questions.q: In this lesson, what does revisiting the shared responsibility model "for compliance" actually mean?
options: Reading the same security OF / security IN split to decide which half of an audit belongs to the provider and which belongs to the customer
Compliance makes the provider responsible for everything, including customer data
The model only applies to technical configuration and has no relevance to audits at all
Replacing the shared responsibility model with a completely different compliance-only framework
questions.explain: The split doesn't change — it's read differently, marking out which half of any compliance audit is the provider's scope and which is the customer's.

questions.q: Why doesn't Azure's ISO 27001 certificate, by itself, make a company's Azure-hosted application compliant with ISO 27001?
options: ISO 27001 does not apply to cloud-hosted applications under any circumstances
Azure's ISO 27001 certificate is not a real, independently audited credential
Azure's certificate covers Microsoft's own infrastructure (security OF the cloud), not the customer's own access controls, encryption settings, or logging configuration
Only AWS, not Azure, holds real compliance certifications
questions.explain: Azure's certification attests to the provider's own infrastructure. The customer's configuration decisions are security IN the cloud and remain entirely the customer's own audit scope.

questions.q: What does "compliance inheritance" actually let an organization's auditor do?
options: Automatically extend the provider's certificate to cover the customer's own configuration
Avoid ever needing to review the customer's access control or encryption settings
Skip auditing the organization entirely because the cloud provider is already certified
Accept the cloud provider's own audited report as proof for the infrastructure layer, instead of independently re-testing the provider's datacenter or hypervisor
questions.explain: Compliance inheritance is a legitimate shortcut for the infrastructure layer only — the provider is treated as a sub-service organization whose own report satisfies that portion of the audit.

questions.q: In SOC 2 terminology, what is a cloud provider like AWS or Azure referred to as, when a customer's auditor relies on the provider's own audited controls?
options: A sub-service organization
A primary auditor
A certification body
A compliance officer
questions.explain: SOC 2 language calls a vendor whose controls another organization's audit relies on a sub-service organization.

questions.q: Where would you actually go to pull AWS's own SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certificate to hand to an auditor?
options: A support ticket filed with AWS, with no self-service option available
The customer's own internal policy documents
There is no way to obtain AWS's own compliance reports
AWS Artifact, a self-service portal built into the AWS console
questions.explain: AWS Artifact is the self-service console portal for downloading AWS's own compliance reports and certificates; Microsoft's equivalent is the Service Trust Portal.
